title: TB6-18632
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellant appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant") claims to be a citizen of Afghanistan and no other country. The Appellant appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. The Appellant has tendered new evidence in this appeal. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision and substitute a determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or return the matter to the RPD to be heard by a differently constituted panel.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is denied. Background

The Appellant alleges before the RPD that she is XXXX XXXX, a 28-year-old citizen of Afghanistan who was born on XXXX XXXX, 1987 in XXXX, Saudia Arabia. She states that she does not have citizenship in Saudi Arabia, but that she does hold citizenship in Pakistan through forged documents. She further alleged that she holds Afghan citizenship because her parents were born there, and they hold citizenship there.

The Appellant alleges that, in 1980, her father realized that it was too dangerous for the family to continue to live in Afghanistan, so they moved to Pakistan. She alleges that her father realized that the family would not be able to obtain citizenship in Pakistan, so he decided to improperly obtain Pakistani passports through bribery, move to Saudi Arabia in 1981 and pretend to be Sunni. She states that her family followed the sponsorship system in Saudi Arabia in order to work there.

She alleged that her father's kafil (Saudi sponsor) was growing older and indicated that his son, XXXX, would act as the kafil for the family. A kafil is necessary for foreign workers to live and work in Saudi Arabia. The Appellant states that XXXX wanted her to work for him and become his spouse, or else his kaniz (sex slave). Her father delayed the requests made by XXXX as long as possible.

The Appellant applied for a U.S. visa and traveled to the U.S. in XXXX of 2015 to see her sister. While in the U.S., her father called her and told her not to return to Saudi Arabia because XXXX stated that he would not extend their sponsorship, and the Saudis were deporting people they suspected of being Shia. He also stated that returning to Afghanistan was not an option because it would be interpreted as her father wanting to reassert his claim to their property and that she would be at risk.

While she was in the U.S., the Appellant submitted an application for a Canadian Visitor's Visa (CVV) through a Canadian Visa Application Center in New York. The application was signed on XXXX XXXX, 2015. It was submitted and refused. She entered Canada illegally, crossing the border in Vancouver, British Columbia on XXXX XXXX, 2016. She filed an inland claim in Etobicoke, Ontario on March 11th, 2016. She alleges that she cannot live safely in Afghanistan, Pakistan or Saudi Arabia.
The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim finding that the Appellant was not credible and that she had not established her personal identity.
The Appellant submits that the RPD's credibility and identity finding are flawed.

The RAD finds that the Federal Court of Appeal's decision, in Huruglica,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. In accordance with the decision of the Court, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision to determine if the RPD erred and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. MERITS OF THE APPEAL Admissibility of New Evidence Presented on Appeal

As provided for in s. 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and refugee claimant. Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

The Appellant has submitted a personal affidavit together with exhibits as proposed new evidence with his Appellant's Record. In particular, the Appellant submits Exhibit "F" of the affidavit, a letter from the Afghan Consulate in Toronto confirming they issued an Afghan passport to the Appellant, and Exhibit "I" of the affidavit, the Appellant's Afghan tazkira, as proposed new evidence.

The RAD's analysis of the admissibility of the proposed new evidence must begin first with the test set out in s. 110(4). While the RAD agrees with the Appellant that further analysis of the evidence is required before the RAD can accept the proposed new evidence, the analysis as set out in Raza2 is not entirely appropriate for the purpose of assessing evidence submitted to the RAD. In this regard, the RAD is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Singh.3
Accordingly, the RAD has adapted the analysis in Raza to the assessment of evidence submitted to the RAD.

In assessing whether the proposed new evidence meets the statutory provisions of s. 110(4), the RAD considered the following: (a) First, did the evidence arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim? Here, the RAD may consider whether the evidence is capable of proving the current state of affairs in the country of feared persecution, or an event that occurred or a circumstance that arose after the rejection of the refugee claim.4 (b) The RAD will consider not only the date on which the document came into existence, but the timing of the event or circumstance which the document seeks to prove.5 For example, an affidavit or newspaper article may have been created after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, but the information in the document may be several years old, and the RAD may therefore find that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claim, despite the date of the document. (c) It is important to note here that s. 110(4) does not contemplate whether the evidence arose after the RPD hearing, but rather after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. Where a document arose after the hearing but before the rejection of the refugee claim, it is necessary for the RAD to consider whether the Appellant could have presented the document to the RPD by way of a post-hearing submission. (d) If the evidence is capable of proving an event that occurred or circumstances that arose after the RPD hearing, then the evidence must be considered, and the RAD will proceed to assess the credibility, relevance, and materiality of the document.6 (e) Second, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, it must consider the next factor in s. 110(4). If the evidence is capable of proving only an event that occurred or circumstances that arose prior to the rejection, has the Appellant established that the evidence was not reasonably available for presentation to the RPD before it rejected the claim7 or that it proves a fact that was unknown to him at the time of the hearing?8 If so, the RAD will proceed to assess the newness, credibility and relevance of the evidence. (f) Third, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim and that it was reasonably available at the time of the rejection, it must consider the final part of the s. 110(4) test: could the Appellant reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence prior to the rejection of the refugee claim? If so, the evidence need not be considered.9 If the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to present the evidence to the RPD, the RAD will proceed to assess the newness, credibility, and relevance of the evidence. (g) If the proposed new evidence meets the tests set out in the statutory requirements and in Raza,10 the evidence will be admitted as evidence in the appeal. The materiality of the evidence will be considered in the context of the assessment made under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

The Appellant submits that her proposed new evidence is admissible as evidence in this appeal because she could not reasonably have been expected to have tendered it at the time of the rejection of her claim. She argues that the letter from the consulate confirming they issued her a passport (Exhibit "F" of the affidavit) meets the requirements for new evidence because she was not aware that the RPD would give no weight to her Afghan passport until her claim was rejected. She further submits that exhibit "I" of her affidavit,11 her Afghan tazkira, meets the requirements of new evidence because she did acquire it until after the rejection of her claim.

The RAD finds that the Appellant could not reasonably have anticipated that the RPD would reject her Afghan passport and other evidence with regard to her alleged afghan identity. Accordingly, the RAD finds that the proposed new evidence meets the statutory requirements to be admitted as new evidence in this appeal. The RAD finds that the proposed new evidence also meets the Raza factors. Accordingly, the proposed new evidence is admitted as new evidence in this appeal. The RAD finds that the affidavit itself is not new evidence as it is largely further explanation of her evidence in response to the RPD's findings of fact and, as such, is not new evidence. The RAD finds that only those portions of the affidavit which address Exhibits "f" and "h" of the affidavit is admitted as new evidence in this appeal. Oral Hearing

Subsection 110(3) of the IRPA requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD's record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellant. According to subsection 110(6), the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. When read together, subsections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new evidence (i.e., evidence admitted under subsection 110(4), subsection 110(5) or Minister's evidence), in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The new evidence admitted in this appeal are documents which the Appellant has argued raise a new issue with regard to her identity. The RPD did not access the merits of the claim after finding that the Appellant had not established her identity. The RAD notes that, while the new evidence may address the Appellant's identity, the new evidence would not justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim, as the merits of the claim were not assessed. As the new evidence cannot justify either allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim, then it does not meet the requirements of 110(6). Each of the requirements in 110(6)(a) through (c) have to be met, and in this case the requirement in 110(6)(c) is not met. As such, the RAD has no discretion to hold a hearing.

The determinative issue in this appeal is whether the Appellant has established her identity which in the context of refugee law includes not only the name or names the Appellant uses or has used, but also includes citizenship(s), country of origin, age, race and ethnicity.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: In order to establish her identity before the RPD, the Appellant relied on his testimony and the following personalized documents: (a) Pakistani passport, dated XXXX XXXX, 2012, showing XXXX, PAKISTAN as the place of birth and bearing the name XXXX12 (b) Afghan passport, dated XXXX XXXX, 2016, bearing the name XXXX XXXX13 (c) U.S. visa, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015, bearing the name FNUXXXX XXXX (FNU being: First Name Unknown)14 (d) Notice of Seizure IMM 5265 bearing the name of XXXX XXXX15 (e) Use of Representative Form IMM 5476 bearing the name of XXXX XXXX16 (f) Generic Application Form IMM 0008, Schedule 12 IMM 5669 and Schedule A Background Declaration bearing the name of XXXX XXXX17 (g) Basis of Claim Form bearing the name of XXXX XXXX18 (h) Canadian Visitor's Visa Application bearing the name of XXXX XXXXwith parents names identified as: XXXX and XXXX XXXX19 (i) Kingdom of Saudi Arabia Residence Permit bearing the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX20 (j) Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Saudi Commission for Health Specialties Professional Registration ID as a General Dentist bearing the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX21 (k) Kingdom of Saudi Arabia birth certificate and bearing the name of XXXX XXXX (showing parents' nationalities as Pakistani and bearing the names of XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX)22 (l) Afghan identity card bearing the name of XXXX23 (m) Afghan identity card bearing the name of XXXX24 (n) Afghan Secondary School Diploma bearing the name of XXXX son of XXXX25 (o) Power of Attorney, dated May 25th, 2015, bearing the names of XXXX and XXXX26

The Appellant has also tendered additional documents to establish her identity which have been admitted as new evidence in this appeal: 1. A letter from the Afghan Consulate of Toronto in which the consulate confirms that it issued a passport to the Appellant in the name XXXX XXXX27 and which states that she was born in XXXX, Saudi Arabia; and 2. A copy of an Afghan tazkira which states she was born in XXXX XXXXand that her father's name is listed as XXXX.

The Appellant has alleged that she improperly holds citizenship in Pakistan through her parents' forged documents. The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony with regard to her Pakistan citizenship was not credible. In particular, the RPD found that the Appellant's testimony with regard to how she acquired citizenship in Pakistan was not credible. The Appellant alleged that, although she had been issued more than one Pakistani passport in her life, they had been improperly obtained by her father. The RPD found that the Appellant provided various explanations with respect to her Pakistani passport and the alleged timing and manner of her learning that it was improperly obtained. The RPD found that it is more likely the case than not that, if the Pakistani passport was improperly obtained, she was aware prior to any of the travels, including her current trips in order to visit her sister in Dubai, which is contrary to her allegations that she did not know until she arrived in Canada. Given the ease with which she has travelled internationally including the U.S., the RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Pakistani passport is a genuine passport and that she does hold Pakistani citizenship.

The RAD notes that the Appellant does not challenge the RPD's credibility findings regarding how the Appellant alleges she came to possess a Pakistani passport. The Appellant does argue, however, that the RPD's finding about the genuineness of the passport is flawed. She argues that both the Minister and the Canadian Immigration Official who examined the Pakistani passport are of the belief that the passport is not genuine. Furthermore, she argues that the RPD's Reasons are internally inconsistent. [47] ... The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that she more likely than not actively and knowingly travelled using a fraudulently obtained Pakistani passport of her own free will simply to travel to visit family in Dubai. Accordingly, the panel does not accept, on a balance of probabilities, her evidence regarding the alleged false Pakistani passport or the timing of her alleged knowledge that it was improper. Given the ease with which she has travelled, the panel finds that the claimant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Pakistani passport is not a genuine travel document and that she does not hold Pakistani citizenship.28

While it is true that the RPD's Reasons could have been more clearly written and that they do have the appearance of being internally inconsistent, the RAD finds that the RPD's finding in this paragraph must be taken into context of the RPD with the preceding paragraphs of the RPD's Reasons. [44] The panel has considered the various explanations offered by the claimant with respect to her Pakistani passport and the alleged timing and manner of her learning that it was improperly obtained and found to be inauthentic. The panel notes that her narrative suggests that the improper Pakistani passport was common knowledge within her family dating back to the 1980s. [45] The panel finds her different versions irreconcilable. The panel further finds that it is more likely the case than not that, if the Pakistani passport was improperly obtained, she was aware prior to any of the travels including her current trips in order to visit her sister in Dubai. Accordingly, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant knowingly travelled to various countries with an allegedly improperly obtained Pakistani passport on a number of occasions before her travel to the U.S. and that she did so without any problems at customs.29

The RAD finds that it is clear that the RPD did not accept the Appellant's allegations that the Pakistani passport was fraudulently obtained. The RAD finds that the intent of the RPD's finding was to demonstrate that the Appellant's allegation that the Pakistani passport was improperly obtained and that she did not know it was not genuine until she arrived in Canada made no sense in light of her previous testimony. After its own review and assessment of the evidence, the RAD agrees with the RPD's findings in this regard.

The RAD further finds that the belief held by the Minister's representative and the Canadian immigration official with regard to the genuineness of the Pakistani passport was based on the allegations made by the Appellant that her passport was improperly obtained. The RAD notes that the Canadian Immigration official indicated that the passport was suspected as being fraudulent but finds that was based on the declaration of the Appellant and not on the basis of a forensic analysis. The RAD further notes that, while the Minister's representative maintains the position that the Pakistani passport is a forged/improperly obtained passport, it only holds that position because the Appellant has alleged that it was obtained through bribery and for no other reason. The RAD notes that the Minister states in its Notice of Intervention in this appeal that the passport was not tampered with or physically altered.30 The RAD further notes that there is no forensic or other evidence to establish that the Pakistani passport is not a genuine document.

The RAD finds that given the uncontested adverse credibility findings with regard to how the Appellant alleges she obtained her Pakistani passport and her willingness and ability to travel internationally on numerous occasions including to the US without any concern being raised with regard to the genuineness of her passport, the RAD agrees with the RPD and finds that the Pakistani passport is a genuine passport. The RAD further finds, by virtue of her ability to acquire and use a genuinely issued Pakistani passport and on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant holds citizenship in Pakistan.

Although the RPD gave little weight to her Afghan passport issued in XXXX 2016 based upon inconsistencies with her explanation about how she obtained the passport and the objective evidence, the Appellant's new evidence31 makes it clear that she was genuinely issued a passport. The RAD notes, however, that citizenship in Afghanistan does not preclude the Appellant from holding citizenship in another country. The RAD notes that the Afghan passport and Pakistani passport bear different surnames.

The RAD notes that the Appellant has tendered a number of documents which bear many different names for her and her parents. She has tendered a tazkira as new evidence to explain some of the variations in the names provided on the documents. The RAD finds, however, that it can give little weight to this document. The RAD notes that the place of birth indicated on the tazkira is XXXX XXXX (Saudi Arabia). The RAD notes the objective evidence in the record with regard to the issuance of tazkiras states that [t]he "place of birth" field on a tazkira refers to the birthplace of the applicant's father. The Appellant alleges her father and mother were born in Afghanistan.

The RAD finds that the Appellant has not established her identity, on a balance of probabilities. At best, she holds citizenship in two different countries under different names: Pakistan and Afghanistan. While she alleged that she cannot return to either country, the RAD notes that her allegations with regard to Pakistan relate to her allegations that her citizenship there was gained by the use of fraudulent documents and that she has no right to citizenship. The RAD has found that those allegations are not credible and that she does have genuine citizenship. At worst, she has not established that the documents she tendered can be relied upon to establish her identity. The RAD further finds that, given the Appellant's credibility has been undermined, her testimony cannot be relied upon to establish her identity.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant has failed to provide sufficient reliable documents and credible evidence to establish her identity, as required by section 106 of the IRPA and Rule 11 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.32 The burden of establishing identity must be satisfied before the panel goes on to consider the merits of the claim and whether the Appellant, in this case, faces a serious possibility of being persecuted or is a person in need of protection.

In the alternative, the RAD finds that the Appellant has citizenship in Pakistan but has not established that she faces a serious possibility of being persecuted or is a person in need of protection in Pakistan.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the Refugee Appeal Division confirms the decision of the Refugee Protection Division. The Appellant's appeal is denied.
